CausalChain: Excessive alcohol consumption -> Generation of acetaldehyde and reactive oxygen species -> Genetic predisposition (e.g., PNPLA3 risk allele) compromises lipid metabolism -> Alcohol induces gut dysbiosis, reducing butyrate-producing bacteria -> Loss of gut barrier integrity -> Increased intestinal permeability -> Elevated translocation of LPS to the liver -> Activation of Kupffer cells via TLR4/NF-κB signaling -> Chronic inflammation and hepatic stellate cell activation -> Accelerated fibrosis and oncogenic milieu -> Development of hepatocellular carcinoma
Hypothesis: In patients with alcohol-associated liver disease, the interplay between the PNPLA3 risk allele and alcohol-induced depletion of butyrate-producing gut bacteria synergistically increases intestinal permeability and LPS-driven inflammatory signaling, thereby accelerating fibrosis and increasing the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. Restoring the abundance of butyrate-producing microbiota may therefore serve as a novel therapeutic strategy to reduce HCC risk in this population.
Abstract: Alcohol-associated liver disease is a multifactorial condition in which heavy alcohol intake, concomitant metabolic derangements, and genetic predispositions converge to promote liver inflammation, fibrosis, and ultimately hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Recent evidence highlights the role of gut dysbiosis in mediating these processes, particularly the reduction of butyrate-producing bacterial taxa which compromises intestinal barrier integrity. We propose that in patients with alcohol-associated liver disease, the presence of risk alleles such as those in PNPLA3, when compounded by an alcohol-induced loss of beneficial, anti‐inflammatory gut microbiota, leads to enhanced lipopolysaccharide (LPS) translocation and exaggerated toll‐like receptor 4 (TLR4) signaling. This “double hit” creates a pro‐inflammatory microenvironment that accelerates hepatic stellate cell activation, fibrosis, and oncogenic transformation. Our hypothesis posits that targeted interventions to restore butyrate-producing bacteria and modulate the gut-liver axis may mitigate HCC risk in genetically susceptible individuals.
